strengths: First rigorous theoretical analysis of Muon's training dynamics and scaling laws with concrete exponential vs. polynomial speedup results (Theorems 4.1-4.2) and superior power-law scaling (Theorems 5.7-5.8)

Novel preconditioning perspective (Section 6) interpreting Muon as implicit matrix preconditioner with task alignment, including insightful analysis of why Muon works without explicit task structure knowledge
Technically rigorous and complete: careful treatment of asymptotic analysis, detailed proofs in appendices, multiple analytical techniques (SVD analysis, phase transition analysis, linear stability)

Multi-faceted experimental validation spanning theoretical model (numerical simulations), synthetic imbalanced classification (MNIST), and realistic LLM pre-training demonstrating broad applicability of key insights
Well-organized presentation with clear theorem statements, effective use of main text vs. appendix, and insightful mechanism explanations (e.g., Lemma 6.1 on matrix sign approximating identity)
Comprehensive analysis across multiple regimes: noiseless, noisy with fixed groups, and power-law frequency scaling, providing broad theoretical coverage
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Linear softmax associative memory is far simplified from real deep learning; LLaMA scaling slopes (-1.13 vs -0.66) substantially less dramatic than theory predicts, suggesting important missing factors not captured by model

Restrictive assumptions: Strict orthogonal embeddings assumption, hierarchical discrete frequency grouping, and asymptotic K→∞, M→∞ regime may not reflect realistic problems; robustness to perturbations unclear

Limited baseline comparisons: Analysis focuses on GD which is known to struggle with imbalance; no theoretical or experimental comparison with practical adaptive methods (Adam, AdamW) limiting relevance
Simplified noise model: Uniform random label corruption (Eq. 1) unrealistic; robustness to structured noise patterns (e.g., confusions between similar classes) unknown

Asymptotic vs. finite-sample: Heavy reliance on K→∞ limits with o_K(1) terms; explicit finite-K behavior and practical guidance on when theory applies missing; learning rate selection impractical (e.g., η = Θ(log K/T))

Incomplete formalization and clarity: Theorem 6.4 marked 'informal'; phase transition analysis (Section E.2) complex with many technical bounds (e.g., |s̃_{t,l}| ≤ 2M/C) lacking intuition for tightness; conditions for phase transitions have limited explanation
Limited experimental scope: LLaMA experiments use only 100M parameters; deeper networks might show different scaling; MNIST uses only 2-layer MLP; Figure 2 lacks error bars on slope estimates

Missing practical insights: Unclear when practitioners should use Muon vs. alternatives, parameter regime for applicability, handling of assumption violations (near-orthogonal embeddings), sensitivity to learning rate misspecification

strengths: Novel theoretical characterization of Muon's training dynamics with rigorous analysis covering noiseless case, three-phase noisy dynamics, and scaling laws
Clear intuition for speedup mechanism: Muon learns imbalanced frequency components uniformly while GD scales updates by p_j, causing bottlenecks
Quantitative scaling law results showing O(1/T²) for Muon vs O(1/T^(1-1/β)) for GD under power-law frequency assumptions
Sophisticated mathematical analysis with careful treatment of block-diagonal structures, gradient decomposition, and SVD properties
Preconditioning interpretation connecting Muon to implicit task alignment provides new theoretical perspective
weaknesses: Severely restrictive model: orthogonal embeddings (Assumption 3.1), linear softmax, hierarchical frequency structure (Assumption 3.2), and regime K≫1, M≪√K are unrealistic; relaxation to near-orthogonality mentioned but not analyzed

Weak experimental validation: LLaMA results (Fig. 2) show single run with no error bars, standard deviations, or significance testing; modest 1.7× speedup may be within noise; different hyperparameter tuning per budget confounds comparison

Theory-practice gap: synthetic experiments use 2-layer ReLU MLP fundamentally different from linear associative memory; no empirical verification that real datasets exhibit hierarchical frequency structure; all experiments measure training loss, not generalization

Loose theoretical bounds: GD has only lower bounds Ω̃(log K/T^(1-1/β)), Muon has only upper bounds Õ((log K)²/T²), no matching lower bounds for Muon; constants hidden in Õ notation; material gap between bounds

Limited novelty: core speedup from balancing frequency learning is somewhat expected from spectral normalization literature; no evidence theory explains Muon's success in general settings without hierarchical frequencies

strengths: Addresses important gap in theoretical understanding of Muon optimizer with comprehensive analysis spanning noiseless, noisy, and scaling law regimes
Novel insights into Muon as implicit matrix preconditioner with clear explanation of why matrix-level normalization outperforms element-wise sign
Technically rigorous analysis with sophisticated proof techniques including block-structure SVD decomposition (Proposition B.1) and phase-transition characterization
Experimental validation across multiple settings (numerical simulations, nonlinear MNIST, LLaMA pre-training) demonstrating generalization beyond linear model
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation, intuitive explanations after main theorems, and organized appendix
Key theoretical result showing exponential speedup for Muon over GD in noiseless case and superior scaling law (Õ(T^-2) vs Ω̃(T^-(1-1/β))) in noisy case
weaknesses: Model assumptions are restrictive: linear softmax, orthogonal embeddings (Assumption 3.1), and discretized hierarchical frequency structure (Assumption 3.2) limit applicability to real deep learning
Loose constants in scaling laws with hidden log K factors weaken practical implications; optimal learning rate selection η=Θ(log K/T) requires knowing K and T in advance
Missing computational cost analysis: SVD per iteration adds O(K³) complexity; when does optimization speedup justify this overhead compared to standard GD?
LLaMA experiments limited to single model scale (100M) and data range (4B-10B tokens); missing AdamW baseline which is standard for LLM training; no error bars or confidence intervals shown
TRA-SignGD analysis relies on oracle knowledge of embeddings E, Ẽ making it primarily a theoretical device; practical implications of preconditioning perspective underexplored
Proof techniques are well-executed but relatively standard (SGD analysis, SVD decomposition, phase-based analysis); limited novelty in methodology
Three-phase dynamics analysis involves loose bounds (3M² terms from conservative bounding) and parameter tuning steps that may not be tight
Gap between linear associative memory model and practical Transformers with nonlinear activations, attention, and complex loss landscapes remains substantial despite nonlinear MNIST validation

strengths: Novel theoretical analysis of Muon training dynamics (first of its kind), going beyond just convergence rates to characterize three-phase dynamics and derive scaling laws
Clear mechanistic insights: shows GD learns imbalanced frequency components while Muon equalizes progress through implicit preconditioning
Comprehensive technical analysis spanning noiseless case, noisy dynamics, scaling laws, and preconditioning interpretation with detailed proofs
Thoughtful experimental progression from exact theoretical settings to increasingly realistic tasks (synthetic → MNIST → LLaMA)
Rigorous treatment with careful presentation of assumptions and some empirical investigation of their violations
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: theory assumes linear softmax, orthogonal embeddings, zero initialization, and specific hierarchical frequency structure, while experiments involve nonlinear networks and random initialization

Limited practical impact: paper explains why Muon works but doesn't enable algorithmic improvements or better hyperparameter selection for practitioners

Tightness concerns: heavy use of asymptotic notation (o_K(1), Õ), GD analysis uses stability-based lower bounds rather than matching upper bounds, many hidden constants make bounds' practical relevance unclear

Experimental limitations: synthetic experiments trivially confirm theory; MNIST experiments use shallow networks; LLaMA experiments (100M parameters, 10B tokens) don't validate predicted scaling exponents quantitatively
